questions.title: The urgent account warning
questions.learningObjective: Identify urgency, unexpected requests and mismatched context in a suspicious message
questions.scenario: A message says your learning-platform account will be disabled in 20 minutes unless you sign in through its embedded link. You were not expecting an account notice.
questions.question: What is the safest first response?

options.text: Reply and ask the sender to prove they are an administrator.
Open the platform using a saved bookmark or typed known address, then check notices; report the message if suspicious.
Forward the message to classmates to ask whether they received it.
Use the link immediately so the account is not disabled.

questions.correctAnswer: Open the platform using a saved bookmark or typed known address, then check notices; report the message if suspicious.

A.explanation: Replying engages the sender and does not independently establish identity.

B.explanation: Correct. Independently navigate to the known service instead of trusting the embedded link, and report suspicious mail through the approved channel.

C.explanation: Wider forwarding can spread malicious links and expose recipients; use the approved reporting route.

D.explanation: This follows the message’s pressure and may disclose credentials to a look-alike site.

questions.explanation: Correct. Independently navigate to the known service instead of trusting the embedded link, and report suspicious mail through the approved channel.
questions.keyTakeaway: Pause when a message creates urgency; verify through a channel you already trust.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Do not open the embedded link. Navigate independently to the service and report the message using the organization’s phishing-report process.
questions.difficultyRationale: Beginner level: single-step recognition.

questions.title: The familiar display name
questions.learningObjective: Check the actual sender address and domain rather than relying on display name
questions.scenario: An email displays the name “Campus IT Helpdesk,” but the full sender address ends in an unrelated public email domain. It asks you to confirm your password.
questions.question: Which detail is most useful for assessing the sender?

options.text: The full sender address and domain, checked against a known official contact.
The display name looks familiar.
The email arrived during normal working hours.
The message uses the school logo.

questions.correctAnswer: The full sender address and domain, checked against a known official contact.

A.explanation: Correct. Inspect the full address and verify the domain using an independently known directory or channel.

B.explanation: Display names are easy to choose or imitate and do not authenticate the sender.

C.explanation: Timing is weak evidence; malicious messages can be sent at any time.

D.explanation: Logos can be copied and are not proof of message origin.

questions.explanation: Correct. Inspect the full address and verify the domain using an independently known directory or channel.
questions.keyTakeaway: A familiar name or logo is not identity proof; inspect and independently verify the actual address.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Expand sender details, inspect the full address and domain, and contact IT through the published helpdesk channel if a credential request is unexpected.
questions.difficultyRationale: Beginner level: single-step recognition.

questions.title: The look-alike sign-in link
questions.learningObjective: Inspect a link destination before opening it and navigate independently when uncertain
questions.scenario: A message says you must review a shared document. The visible text says “university portal,” but the underlying link points to a misspelled domain.
questions.question: What should you do?

options.text: Open it in a private browsing window.
Do not use the link; open the known portal independently and locate the document there.
Click because the visible text names the university.
Copy the link into a search engine and open the first result.

questions.correctAnswer: Do not use the link; open the known portal independently and locate the document there.

A.explanation: Private browsing does not make a malicious destination safe.

B.explanation: Correct. Independent navigation avoids relying on a potentially deceptive destination.

C.explanation: Visible link text can conceal a different destination.

D.explanation: Search results may include look-alike or sponsored destinations and do not validate the message.

questions.explanation: Correct. Independent navigation avoids relying on a potentially deceptive destination.
questions.keyTakeaway: Treat a link’s actual destination—not its label—as the relevant address.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Use a bookmark or manually enter the service’s known address. Report the suspicious message if it is unsolicited.
questions.difficultyRationale: Beginner level: single-step recognition.

questions.title: One password, multiple accounts
questions.learningObjective: Avoid password reuse across services and understand credential-stuffing exposure
questions.scenario: You use the same password for a shopping site and your school account. The shopping site reports a data breach.
questions.question: What is the best response for your school account?

options.text: Wait until the school sends a warning.
Keep the password because the school account uses MFA.
Change the reused password to a unique one and review other accounts where it was reused.
Add an exclamation mark to the same password everywhere.

questions.correctAnswer: Change the reused password to a unique one and review other accounts where it was reused.

A.explanation: Waiting leaves an exposed credential in use; address the reuse promptly.

B.explanation: MFA adds protection but does not make password reuse safe; stolen credentials can still be abused.

C.explanation: Correct. A breach at one service can expose a password reused elsewhere; unique credentials limit cross-service compromise.

D.explanation: A predictable minor variation still preserves password reuse and may be guessable.

questions.explanation: Correct. A breach at one service can expose a password reused elsewhere; unique credentials limit cross-service compromise.
questions.keyTakeaway: Use a unique password for every account so one service’s breach does not unlock another.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Change the school password to a unique strong password, change other reused instances, and check account activity.
questions.difficultyRationale: Beginner level: single-step recognition.

questions.title: Managing unique passwords
questions.learningObjective: Use an approved password manager and unique generated credentials
questions.scenario: You have many accounts and struggle to remember a different strong password for each one.
questions.question: Which approach best balances security and usability?

options.text: Use one memorable password for every service.
Keep all passwords in a note on a shared computer desktop.
Send passwords to yourself in email so you can search for them.
Use an organization-approved password manager with a strong protected vault and unique generated passwords.

questions.correctAnswer: Use an organization-approved password manager with a strong protected vault and unique generated passwords.

A.explanation: Reuse creates cross-account risk when any one service is breached.

B.explanation: A shared, unprotected note exposes multiple accounts to anyone with access to the device.

C.explanation: Email may be accessible to mailbox attackers and is not an appropriate password vault.

D.explanation: Correct. An approved manager helps maintain distinct credentials without requiring people to memorize them all.

questions.explanation: Correct. An approved manager helps maintain distinct credentials without requiring people to memorize them all.
questions.keyTakeaway: A trusted password manager supports unique credentials; protect the vault itself carefully.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Use an organization-approved password manager, secure its master authentication, and never store real passwords in the learning simulation.
questions.difficultyRationale: Beginner level: single-step recognition.

questions.title: The one-time code request
questions.learningObjective: Never disclose a one-time password or verification code to another person
questions.scenario: A caller claiming to be bank support says a verification code has been sent to your phone and asks you to read it aloud to stop a suspicious transaction.
questions.question: What should you do?

options.text: Hang up and contact the bank using the number on your card or official app; never share the code.
Read only the first half of the code.
Read the code because the caller knows your name.
Send the code by text instead of saying it aloud.

questions.correctAnswer: Hang up and contact the bank using the number on your card or official app; never share the code.

A.explanation: Correct. An unsolicited caller must not receive an authenticator output; independently contact the institution.

B.explanation: Partial disclosure can still help an attacker complete an authentication flow.

C.explanation: Knowing personal details does not authenticate the caller; the code may authorize an action.

D.explanation: Changing the communication channel does not make disclosure safe.

questions.explanation: Correct. An unsolicited caller must not receive an authenticator output; independently contact the institution.
questions.keyTakeaway: An OTP is an authenticator output. Do not disclose it to callers, chat contacts or anyone else.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: End the call and contact the bank through a known official channel. Review account activity and report the attempted social engineering.
questions.difficultyRationale: Beginner level: single-step recognition.

questions.title: An unexpected sign-in prompt
questions.learningObjective: Deny uninitiated authentication prompts and report repeated unexpected requests
questions.scenario: You are not signing in, but your phone displays an approval request for your work account.
questions.question: What is the safest action?

options.text: Ignore it and approve the next prompt if it appears again.
Deny the request and report it to the helpdesk or security team.
Share a screenshot of the prompt publicly.
Approve it to clear the notification.

questions.correctAnswer: Deny the request and report it to the helpdesk or security team.

A.explanation: Repeated prompts can be an authentication-fatigue tactic; approving a later one is unsafe.

B.explanation: Correct. A prompt you did not initiate may indicate someone has your password or is attempting authentication.

C.explanation: Public sharing may expose account identifiers or organizational information and does not report the incident appropriately.

D.explanation: Approval may authorize an attacker’s login attempt.

questions.explanation: Correct. A prompt you did not initiate may indicate someone has your password or is attempting authentication.
questions.keyTakeaway: Only approve authentication you initiated and can confidently match to your sign-in.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Deny the request, do not disclose any code, and report unexpected or repeated prompts through the organization’s support channel.
questions.difficultyRationale: Beginner level: single-step recognition.

questions.title: The browser certificate warning
questions.learningObjective: Respond safely to browser certificate and security warnings
questions.scenario: While opening a site to pay a fee, the browser displays a certificate warning and says the connection may not be private.
questions.question: What should you do?

options.text: Choose “proceed anyway” because the page looks normal.
Disable browser security checks for the session.
Stop and access the service later through its known official address or contact its support team.
Try the same page repeatedly until the warning disappears.

questions.correctAnswer: Stop and access the service later through its known official address or contact its support team.

A.explanation: A familiar-looking page does not resolve a certificate or connection warning.

B.explanation: Disabling protections increases exposure and is not an appropriate way to complete a payment.

C.explanation: Correct. Do not bypass a browser security warning for a sensitive transaction; verify independently.

D.explanation: Repeated attempts do not establish that the site is trustworthy.

questions.explanation: Correct. Do not bypass a browser security warning for a sensitive transaction; verify independently.
questions.keyTakeaway: Do not bypass a security warning to complete a sensitive task.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Close the page, avoid entering credentials or payment data, and verify the service through a known official route.
questions.difficultyRationale: Beginner level: single-step recognition.

questions.title: The unexpected personal-data form
questions.learningObjective: Share only information necessary for a legitimate and verified purpose
questions.scenario: A person claiming to organize a campus event sends a form requesting your ID number, date of birth, home address and bank details to “confirm attendance.”
questions.question: What is the best response?

options.text: Verify the organizer through the official event channel and ask which fields are necessary before sharing anything.
Submit everything because the event sounds legitimate.
Enter made-up details to get past the form.
Send the information in a private social-media message instead.

questions.correctAnswer: Verify the organizer through the official event channel and ask which fields are necessary before sharing anything.

A.explanation: Correct. Confirm purpose and legitimacy, then disclose only the minimum required information using an approved channel.

B.explanation: A plausible event does not establish the form’s authenticity or justify collecting unrelated sensitive data.

C.explanation: False information can create operational problems and still expose you to malicious links or follow-up requests.

D.explanation: A different channel does not fix an unverified request or excessive data collection.

questions.explanation: Correct. Confirm purpose and legitimacy, then disclose only the minimum required information using an approved channel.
questions.keyTakeaway: Check purpose, legitimacy and necessity before disclosing personal information.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Contact the event organizer using a published official channel. Do not submit unnecessary financial or identity data.
questions.difficultyRationale: Beginner level: single-step recognition.

questions.title: The unexpected invoice attachment
questions.learningObjective: Verify unexpected attachments through a trusted channel before opening
questions.scenario: An email appears to come from a classmate and includes an unexpected file named “Updated_Grades.zip.” The classmate has not mentioned sending it.
questions.question: What should you do first?

options.text: Disable antivirus temporarily if the file is blocked.
Open it to see whether the file is relevant.
Verify with the classmate using a separate known contact method and report the message if unconfirmed.
Forward the attachment to another student to test it.

questions.correctAnswer: Verify with the classmate using a separate known contact method and report the message if unconfirmed.

A.explanation: Disabling protections to open an unexpected file increases risk.

B.explanation: Opening an unexpected archive may expose the device to malicious content.

C.explanation: Correct. A known account can be compromised; confirm an unexpected attachment independently.

D.explanation: Forwarding can spread a malicious file to more people.

questions.explanation: Correct. A known account can be compromised; confirm an unexpected attachment independently.
questions.keyTakeaway: An attachment from a familiar account can still be unsafe or unexpected.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Do not open or forward the file. Verify with the sender using a previously known contact method and follow reporting procedures.
questions.difficultyRationale: Beginner level: single-step recognition.

questions.title: The update link in an email
questions.learningObjective: Install updates through trusted vendor or managed-device mechanisms
questions.scenario: A pop-up email says your laptop is at risk and provides an attached “critical security update” installer.
questions.question: Which action is safest?

options.text: Search for a similar installer on a random download site.
Download the update only through the operating system’s trusted update mechanism or the organization’s managed software portal.
Run the attached installer immediately.
Ask the sender to send the installer in a password-protected archive.

questions.correctAnswer: Download the update only through the operating system’s trusted update mechanism or the organization’s managed software portal.

A.explanation: An unrelated download site may distribute tampered or malicious software.

B.explanation: Correct. Updates should be obtained and authenticated through trusted vendor or managed channels.

C.explanation: Email attachments are not a trusted update channel and may contain malware.

D.explanation: A password-protected archive does not establish provenance or integrity.

questions.explanation: Correct. Updates should be obtained and authenticated through trusted vendor or managed channels.
questions.keyTakeaway: Install updates through trusted, authenticated update mechanisms—not unsolicited links or attachments.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Ignore the email attachment and check the device’s built-in update service or your organization’s managed software portal.
questions.difficultyRationale: Beginner level: single-step recognition.

questions.title: The authority and urgency trick
questions.learningObjective: Recognize manipulation using urgency, authority or familiarity
questions.scenario: A caller says they are the principal’s assistant and demands your class portal password immediately because “the principal has approved it.”
questions.question: What is the safest response?

options.text: Send the password but change it after the call.
Share it because the caller invokes a senior authority.
Ask the caller to repeat the principal’s name.
Refuse to disclose the password and verify the request through an official contact channel.

questions.correctAnswer: Refuse to disclose the password and verify the request through an official contact channel.

A.explanation: Temporary disclosure still compromises the account and may enable immediate access.

B.explanation: Claims of authority are easy to make and do not justify password disclosure.

C.explanation: Knowing a name is not independent identity verification.

D.explanation: Correct. Authority pressure and urgency are common social-engineering cues; passwords should not be shared.

questions.explanation: Correct. Authority pressure and urgency are common social-engineering cues; passwords should not be shared.
questions.keyTakeaway: Authority, familiarity and urgency are persuasion techniques—not proof of identity.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Refuse credential disclosure. End the interaction and confirm any legitimate request through a published contact channel.
questions.difficultyRationale: Beginner level: single-step recognition.

questions.title: The open public Wi-Fi network
questions.learningObjective: Choose safer connection practices and avoid exposing sensitive data on untrusted networks
questions.scenario: At an airport, several similarly named free Wi-Fi networks appear. You need to access a sensitive work account.
questions.question: What is the safest option?

options.text: Use any open network because HTTPS makes every activity safe.
Join the network with the strongest signal.
Use a personal or organization-approved hotspot, or a verified network with required protections.
Turn off the device firewall to improve speed.

questions.correctAnswer: Use a personal or organization-approved hotspot, or a verified network with required protections.

A.explanation: HTTPS protects data in transit to a valid site but does not authenticate the Wi-Fi operator or protect against every threat.

B.explanation: Signal strength does not verify who operates the network.

C.explanation: Correct. Prefer a trusted connection; public wireless networks can expose devices and traffic to additional risk.

D.explanation: Disabling a security control does not improve trust in the network and increases exposure.

questions.explanation: Correct. Prefer a trusted connection; public wireless networks can expose devices and traffic to additional risk.
questions.keyTakeaway: Network names and signal strength do not prove that a Wi-Fi network is legitimate.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Prefer mobile data or an organization-approved hotspot. Follow your organization’s VPN and remote-access requirements.
questions.difficultyRationale: Beginner level: single-step recognition.

questions.title: You clicked a suspicious link
questions.learningObjective: Report suspected phishing or accidental interaction promptly through the approved channel
questions.scenario: You clicked a suspicious link and entered your work password before realizing the page was fake.
questions.question: What should you do next?

options.text: Post the phishing message on social media and ask what to do.
Delete the email and say nothing because you feel embarrassed.
Wait to see whether an alert appears.
Report immediately through the approved security channel and follow instructions to secure the account from a trusted device.

questions.correctAnswer: Report immediately through the approved security channel and follow instructions to secure the account from a trusted device.

A.explanation: Public posting may expose organizational details and does not trigger incident response.

B.explanation: Non-reporting delays containment and may allow the account to be misused.

C.explanation: Waiting can give an attacker more time to use exposed credentials.

D.explanation: Correct. Prompt reporting enables the organization to contain possible credential compromise and assess impact.

questions.explanation: Correct. Prompt reporting enables the organization to contain possible credential compromise and assess impact.
questions.keyTakeaway: Fast, accurate reporting helps limit harm; do not hide accidental interaction.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Contact the security/helpdesk team immediately. From a trusted device, follow their direction to reset credentials, revoke sessions and inspect account activity.
questions.difficultyRationale: Beginner level: single-step recognition.

questions.title: The unexpected QR code
questions.learningObjective: Treat unexpected QR codes as links and verify the destination before proceeding
questions.scenario: A sticker covers the QR code on a parking meter. The replacement code opens a page asking for card details and vehicle information.
questions.question: What should you do?

options.text: Use the official payment app or website reached independently and inspect/report the altered code.
Send the QR code to friends so they can check whether it works.
Scan and pay because the sticker is on the meter.
Enter card details only if the page has the meter operator’s logo.

questions.correctAnswer: Use the official payment app or website reached independently and inspect/report the altered code.

A.explanation: Correct. QR codes conceal URLs; use a known official payment route and report suspected tampering.

B.explanation: Sharing can spread the malicious destination and does not verify its operator.

C.explanation: A sticker can be placed over a legitimate QR code; physical placement does not prove authenticity.

D.explanation: Logos can be copied and do not prove the destination is legitimate.

questions.explanation: Correct. QR codes conceal URLs; use a known official payment route and report suspected tampering.
questions.keyTakeaway: A QR code is simply a link in a different format; inspect and verify it before acting.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Do not enter details on the linked page. Use the operator’s official app or a known address and report the altered sticker.
questions.difficultyRationale: Beginner level: single-step recognition.

questions.title: The targeted project request
questions.learningObjective: Use context, relationship and business-process checks to detect targeted deception
questions.scenario: A message uses your real project name and mentions a current deadline. It asks you to open a shared document and sign in again, but the sender domain differs from the partner’s known domain.
questions.question: Which verification approach is strongest?

options.text: Verify the request with the partner using a previously established contact channel, and access the project system independently.
Open the document on a personal phone instead of a work laptop.
Reply to the message and ask whether it is genuine.
Trust it because the project details are accurate.

questions.correctAnswer: Verify the request with the partner using a previously established contact channel, and access the project system independently.

A.explanation: Correct. Use relationship and workflow context as signals, but authenticate through an independent channel.

B.explanation: Changing devices does not make a deceptive link or credential prompt trustworthy.

C.explanation: A response goes to the potentially compromised sender and does not independently verify the request.

D.explanation: Public or compromised information can make targeted deception convincing; context alone is not authentication.

questions.explanation: Correct. Use relationship and workflow context as signals, but authenticate through an independent channel.
questions.keyTakeaway: Targeted content can be accurate and still fraudulent; independently verify the sender and workflow.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Pause the sign-in request, contact the partner through known contact details, and report the mismatch to the security team.
questions.difficultyRationale: Intermediate level: contextual verification and multi-step judgment.

questions.title: The delivery-fee text
questions.learningObjective: Identify fraudulent SMS requests and verify through independent channels
questions.scenario: You receive an SMS claiming a parcel is held for a small delivery fee. It includes a shortened link and says the parcel will be returned today.
questions.question: What is the best response?

options.text: Reply with your full name and address to identify the parcel.
Open the shortened link because the fee is small.
Forward the SMS to another recipient to see if their parcel is also held.
Use the courier’s official app or independently located website to check tracking; do not use the SMS link.

questions.correctAnswer: Use the courier’s official app or independently located website to check tracking; do not use the SMS link.

A.explanation: Providing personal information to an unverified sender creates additional exposure.

B.explanation: A small payment request can be a pretext to harvest card details or credentials.

C.explanation: Forwarding spreads the lure and does not verify its authenticity.

D.explanation: Correct. Verify parcel status independently rather than following an unsolicited link.

questions.explanation: Correct. Verify parcel status independently rather than following an unsolicited link.
questions.keyTakeaway: Unexpected delivery texts with short links and urgent fees should be checked independently.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Open the courier app or enter its known address yourself. Report and delete the suspicious message according to local procedures.
questions.difficultyRationale: Intermediate level: contextual verification and multi-step judgment.

questions.title: The “IT support” caller
questions.learningObjective: Verify caller identity and resist verbal pressure to disclose data or approve actions
questions.scenario: A caller claiming to be IT support says your laptop is infected and asks you to install a remote-access tool and read out an authentication code.
questions.question: What should you do?

options.text: Share the code but refuse remote access.
Install the tool because IT support needs to troubleshoot.
End the call and contact IT using the organization’s published helpdesk route.
Ask the caller to send a company badge photo.

questions.correctAnswer: End the call and contact IT using the organization’s published helpdesk route.

A.explanation: The code may authorize account access even without remote-control software.

B.explanation: Unverified remote access can give the caller control of the device.

C.explanation: Correct. Independently verify support requests; never disclose authentication outputs to an unsolicited caller.

D.explanation: A photo can be fabricated or copied and is not reliable identity verification.

questions.explanation: Correct. Independently verify support requests; never disclose authentication outputs to an unsolicited caller.
questions.keyTakeaway: Caller ID, technical language and urgency are not proof that a caller is authorized.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: End the call. Contact the helpdesk using a known directory or portal and report the attempted remote-access and code request.
questions.difficultyRationale: Intermediate level: contextual verification and multi-step judgment.

questions.title: The meeting-room QR login
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate QR-linked destinations before authentication or payment
questions.scenario: A QR code on a meeting-room poster promises access to the conference Wi-Fi. After scanning, it opens a sign-in page on a domain unrelated to the venue.
questions.question: What should you do?

options.text: Try the same credentials using a different browser.
Enter your corporate credentials because the poster is inside the office.
Check the displayed URL, close the page, and ask facilities/IT for the official network instructions.
Use a coworker’s login instead.

questions.correctAnswer: Check the displayed URL, close the page, and ask facilities/IT for the official network instructions.

A.explanation: A different browser still submits credentials to the same untrusted site.

B.explanation: The physical location does not validate the QR destination or page operator.

C.explanation: Correct. Verify the destination and obtain connection details through an approved internal source.

D.explanation: Sharing credentials exposes the coworker’s account and does not validate the page.

questions.explanation: Correct. Verify the destination and obtain connection details through an approved internal source.
questions.keyTakeaway: QR codes conceal destinations; assess the actual URL before authenticating.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Do not enter credentials. Confirm the poster with facilities or IT and use the authorized network onboarding process.
questions.difficultyRationale: Intermediate level: contextual verification and multi-step judgment.

questions.title: Repeated MFA prompts
questions.learningObjective: Recognize repeated push prompts as possible account compromise and deny/report them
questions.scenario: Over ten minutes, your authenticator sends repeated sign-in approval prompts. You are not attempting to sign in, and a coworker says to approve one to stop them.
questions.question: What is the safest response?

options.text: Turn off MFA permanently to stop the notifications.
Share the prompt details in a public chat to ask for help.
Approve one request and then change your password later.
Deny the prompts, stop interacting with them and contact the security team immediately.

questions.correctAnswer: Deny the prompts, stop interacting with them and contact the security team immediately.

A.explanation: Disabling MFA removes a protection and does not address the attempted sign-in.

B.explanation: Public disclosure may reveal account details and will not trigger formal incident response.

C.explanation: Approving may complete an attacker’s login; later action may be too late.

D.explanation: Correct. Repeated uninitiated prompts can be authentication fatigue and may indicate a password is already known to an attacker.

questions.explanation: Correct. Repeated uninitiated prompts can be authentication fatigue and may indicate a password is already known to an attacker.
questions.keyTakeaway: Repeated uninitiated prompts are a possible compromise signal, not a harmless notification problem.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Deny every uninitiated prompt and report immediately. Follow the identity team’s instructions for password reset, session revocation and authenticator review.
questions.difficultyRationale: Intermediate level: contextual verification and multi-step judgment.

questions.title: The macro-enabled invoice
questions.learningObjective: Avoid enabling active content in untrusted documents and verify the sender
questions.scenario: A supplier sends an invoice document you were not expecting. When opened in a preview, it asks you to “Enable Content” to display the invoice.
questions.question: What is the correct response?

options.text: Enable content while disconnected from Wi-Fi.
Verify the invoice with the supplier through known contact details and report the suspicious request; do not enable content.
Upload the file to a public malware-scanning website.
Enable content because invoices often require macros.

questions.correctAnswer: Verify the invoice with the supplier through known contact details and report the suspicious request; do not enable content.

A.explanation: Disconnecting does not make untrusted active content safe; it may still alter or persist on the device.

B.explanation: Correct. Unexpected documents and requests to enable active content require independent verification.

C.explanation: Uploading a business document publicly may disclose confidential data; use organization-approved analysis channels.

D.explanation: Unexpected active content can execute code and should not be enabled simply to view a document.

questions.explanation: Correct. Unexpected documents and requests to enable active content require independent verification.
questions.keyTakeaway: Do not enable macros or active content in an unexpected document to reveal what it contains.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Close the document without enabling content. Verify with the supplier using a known contact method and use approved security analysis if needed.
questions.difficultyRationale: Intermediate level: contextual verification and multi-step judgment.

questions.title: Signals of account takeover
questions.learningObjective: Identify account-takeover signals and initiate trusted account-recovery steps
questions.scenario: You receive an email alert for a successful login from an unfamiliar location. Your account recovery email and forwarding rules also appear to have changed.
questions.question: What is the strongest next step?

options.text: Click the alert email’s “secure account” link and sign in.
Delete the forwarding rule and assume the account is safe.
Use a known official account-recovery route from a trusted device, contact support/security and report the unauthorized changes.
Wait for another alert to confirm the activity.

questions.correctAnswer: Use a known official account-recovery route from a trusted device, contact support/security and report the unauthorized changes.

A.explanation: The alert itself may be spoofed; its link should not be trusted without verification.

B.explanation: A single change does not address potentially stolen credentials, active sessions or other persistence.

C.explanation: Correct. Treat the signals as possible account compromise and use trusted recovery and containment procedures.

D.explanation: Waiting may allow the intruder to maintain access or intercept future messages.

questions.explanation: Correct. Treat the signals as possible account compromise and use trusted recovery and containment procedures.
questions.keyTakeaway: Unexpected logins plus changed recovery settings are strong account-compromise indicators.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Contact the service or organizational identity team using a known route. Follow instructions to secure credentials, sessions, recovery methods and mailbox rules.
questions.difficultyRationale: Intermediate level: contextual verification and multi-step judgment.

questions.title: The broad sharing link
questions.learningObjective: Apply least-privilege and verify recipient, channel and classification before sharing
questions.scenario: A project teammate asks you to upload a spreadsheet containing student IDs and contact details to a folder with “Anyone with the link can view” access.
questions.question: What is the best response?

options.text: Share only with the verified people who need it, using an approved restricted channel and minimum necessary data.
Create the public link but remove the folder next week.
Rename the spreadsheet so it no longer looks sensitive.
Send the file to a personal email account instead.

questions.correctAnswer: Share only with the verified people who need it, using an approved restricted channel and minimum necessary data.

A.explanation: Correct. Verify recipients and classification, then apply least privilege to access and content.

B.explanation: Temporary broad exposure is still exposure; access should be appropriately restricted before sharing.

C.explanation: Renaming does not remove sensitive content or limit access.

D.explanation: A personal mailbox may bypass organizational controls and create a new disclosure path.

questions.explanation: Correct. Verify recipients and classification, then apply least privilege to access and content.
questions.keyTakeaway: Share the minimum necessary data with verified recipients using access controls appropriate to its sensitivity.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Confirm the business need and recipient list, use the approved storage service, disable public access, and set access expiry or review where supported.
questions.difficultyRationale: Intermediate level: contextual verification and multi-step judgment.

questions.title: The suspected malware click
questions.learningObjective: Select appropriate reporting, containment and evidence-preservation steps
questions.scenario: You opened a suspicious attachment on a managed laptop. The device is behaving unusually, and your organization has an incident-response number.
questions.question: What should you do first?

options.text: Post the suspicious file to a public forum for identification.
Immediately follow the organization’s incident procedure, report the event, and isolate the device if policy or responders direct you to.
Delete all suspicious files and clear event logs.
Continue working and run random cleanup utilities.

questions.correctAnswer: Immediately follow the organization’s incident procedure, report the event, and isolate the device if policy or responders direct you to.

A.explanation: Public upload may disclose confidential information and spread malware.

B.explanation: Correct. Prompt reporting and coordinated containment are safer than improvising remediation.

C.explanation: Deleting files or logs can destroy evidence needed for investigation.

D.explanation: Continuing activity or using unapproved tools can worsen impact or interfere with response.

questions.explanation: Correct. Prompt reporting and coordinated containment are safer than improvising remediation.
questions.keyTakeaway: Report quickly and follow the incident-response plan; do not improvise forensic actions.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Contact the organization’s security team immediately. Follow their containment instructions and preserve the device and relevant details.
questions.difficultyRationale: Intermediate level: contextual verification and multi-step judgment.

questions.title: The productivity extension
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate extension permissions, provenance and necessity before installation
questions.scenario: A browser extension promises to summarize every page. It requests permission to read and change all data on every website, including internal work portals.
questions.question: What should you do?

options.text: Use a coworker’s installed extension profile.
Install it only in a private browser window.
Check organizational approval, publisher provenance, necessity and permission scope before installation.
Install it because it has many positive ratings.

questions.correctAnswer: Check organizational approval, publisher provenance, necessity and permission scope before installation.

A.explanation: Using another person’s profile does not resolve the extension’s access or policy risks.

B.explanation: Private mode does not necessarily prevent an extension from accessing permitted page content.

C.explanation: Correct. Broad access to every site creates significant data and account exposure and should be justified and approved.

D.explanation: Ratings do not establish the publisher’s trustworthiness or justify broad permissions.

questions.explanation: Correct. Broad access to every site creates significant data and account exposure and should be justified and approved.
questions.keyTakeaway: An extension with broad permissions can access sensitive page data; assess source and scope before use.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Do not install until the extension is approved and its permissions are proportionate to a documented need.
questions.difficultyRationale: Intermediate level: contextual verification and multi-step judgment.

questions.title: The anonymous cloud folder
questions.learningObjective: Configure sharing permissions and expiry consistent with data sensitivity
questions.scenario: A team shares a folder containing internal project documents through an anonymous link that never expires. The folder is no longer being actively used.
questions.question: Which control change is most appropriate?

options.text: Restrict access to named authorized accounts, set an expiry/review date and remove obsolete access.
Change the folder name and leave permissions unchanged.
Post the link in a team chat so everyone knows where it is.
Keep the link because it is convenient for former collaborators.

questions.correctAnswer: Restrict access to named authorized accounts, set an expiry/review date and remove obsolete access.

A.explanation: Correct. Restrict identities and duration, and review existing permissions according to data sensitivity.

B.explanation: A folder name does not change who can access its content.

C.explanation: Wider distribution increases exposure and does not establish authorization.

D.explanation: Convenience does not justify indefinite anonymous access.

questions.explanation: Correct. Restrict identities and duration, and review existing permissions according to data sensitivity.
questions.keyTakeaway: Cloud sharing should be identity-bound, least-privilege and time-limited when appropriate.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Remove anonymous access, grant only necessary users or groups, set expiry where available and periodically review permissions.
questions.difficultyRationale: Intermediate level: contextual verification and multi-step judgment.

questions.title: The changed supplier bank account
questions.learningObjective: Independently verify changed payment instructions using a known contact method
questions.scenario: A regular supplier emails an updated invoice with new bank details and says payment must be made today to avoid a penalty.
questions.question: What should accounts payable do before changing the beneficiary?

options.text: Call the supplier using the phone number printed in the new email.
Reply to the email asking the sender to confirm the new details.
Pay a small test amount to see whether the account is valid.
Verify the change through a separately established phone number or approved vendor portal and follow dual-approval controls.

questions.correctAnswer: Verify the change through a separately established phone number or approved vendor portal and follow dual-approval controls.

A.explanation: The email may provide an attacker-controlled number; use contact details already on file.

B.explanation: If the account is compromised, the attacker may confirm their own fraudulent instructions.

C.explanation: A test payment still sends funds to an unverified beneficiary and can create loss.

D.explanation: Correct. Payment changes need independent verification through trusted records and the normal authorization process.

questions.explanation: Correct. Payment changes need independent verification through trusted records and the normal authorization process.
questions.keyTakeaway: Never trust changed payment instructions solely because they arrive in a familiar email thread.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Freeze the change until independently verified using contact information already on file, and apply the organization’s payment authorization controls.
questions.difficultyRationale: Intermediate level: contextual verification and multi-step judgment.

questions.title: The unsolicited password-reset link
questions.learningObjective: Use official account-recovery paths and reject unsolicited reset links
questions.scenario: You receive a password-reset SMS for a service while you are not attempting to reset your password. A second message asks you to approve the reset.
questions.question: What should you do?

options.text: Forward the reset code to the number that sent the SMS.
Ignore the link, navigate independently to the service and review account security or contact support if needed.
Approve the reset and immediately choose a new password.
Tap the reset link to see which account it concerns.

questions.correctAnswer: Ignore the link, navigate independently to the service and review account security or contact support if needed.

A.explanation: The code may authorize an attacker-controlled reset.

B.explanation: Correct. Unsolicited reset messages should be verified through the official service rather than followed.

C.explanation: Approving a reset you did not request may give another party control of the account.

D.explanation: The link could lead to a credential-harvesting site.

questions.explanation: Correct. Unsolicited reset messages should be verified through the official service rather than followed.
questions.keyTakeaway: Only initiate recovery yourself through the official service; do not approve an unsolicited reset.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Do not open the SMS link or share a code. Access the service independently and report repeated or suspicious recovery activity.
questions.difficultyRationale: Intermediate level: contextual verification and multi-step judgment.

questions.title: The shared-space work session
questions.learningObjective: Protect remote sessions, devices and information in mixed work environments
questions.scenario: You are working in a shared café. Your laptop is unlocked while you step away, a sensitive dashboard is visible, and you are connected to public Wi-Fi.
questions.question: Which plan best reduces the combined risk?

options.text: Leave the laptop open but minimize the dashboard.
Lock the device before stepping away, keep it physically controlled, use a trusted connection and follow remote-access policy.
Disable screen lock because the café is busy.
Ask a nearby stranger to watch the laptop.

questions.correctAnswer: Lock the device before stepping away, keep it physically controlled, use a trusted connection and follow remote-access policy.

A.explanation: Minimizing a window does not protect the unattended device or session.

B.explanation: Correct. Physical access, screen exposure and network risks require layered controls.

C.explanation: Removing automatic locking increases the opportunity for unauthorized access.

D.explanation: An unknown bystander is not an appropriate security control.

questions.explanation: Correct. Physical access, screen exposure and network risks require layered controls.
questions.keyTakeaway: Remote work combines physical, visual and network risks; use layered protection.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Lock the screen whenever unattended, keep devices in your control, avoid exposing sensitive content and use the approved secure connection method.
questions.difficultyRationale: Intermediate level: contextual verification and multi-step judgment.

questions.title: The QR-code APK download
questions.learningObjective: Assess app-store provenance and permission scope when QR prompts an app install
questions.scenario: A QR code on a delivery notice opens a page asking you to download an Android package file directly because the “official app store is unavailable.”
questions.question: What is the safest decision?

options.text: Do not sideload it; verify the delivery through the courier’s official app or independently located website.
Install the file because the QR code is printed on a delivery notice.
Send the file to a friend to test on their phone.
Install it but deny location permission.

questions.correctAnswer: Do not sideload it; verify the delivery through the courier’s official app or independently located website.

A.explanation: Correct. Use an authenticated distribution channel and independently verify the delivery request.

B.explanation: The printed notice does not authenticate the source or integrity of the installation file.

C.explanation: This transfers risk to another person and may propagate malware.

D.explanation: One permission choice does not make an untrusted package safe; it may request more later or contain malicious code.

questions.explanation: Correct. Use an authenticated distribution channel and independently verify the delivery request.
questions.keyTakeaway: Do not install an unsolicited app package from a QR-linked page; use a trusted app distribution channel.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Close the page, do not install the package, and verify shipment status through the courier’s independently accessed official service.
questions.difficultyRationale: Intermediate level: contextual verification and multi-step judgment.

questions.title: The executive payment exception
questions.learningObjective: Corroborate high-impact requests and payment or credential changes outside email
questions.scenario: A senior executive emails finance from a plausible account and asks for an urgent confidential transfer to a new beneficiary. The message says normal approval can be bypassed because the deal is sensitive.
questions.question: Which control response is strongest?

options.text: Process it because the sender is senior and the request is confidential.
Transfer a smaller amount first to test the beneficiary.
Hold the transfer and verify through a pre-established independent channel and mandatory dual-authorization process.
Reply to the email and request a voice confirmation.

questions.correctAnswer: Hold the transfer and verify through a pre-established independent channel and mandatory dual-authorization process.

A.explanation: Authority and secrecy are not substitutes for identity verification or delegated financial authorization.

B.explanation: A smaller unverified transfer is still unauthorized and may confirm that the account is active.

C.explanation: Correct. High-impact payment instructions require independent corroboration and policy-based approval, regardless of apparent seniority.

D.explanation: A compromised mailbox can be controlled by the attacker, including replies in the same thread.

questions.explanation: Correct. High-impact payment instructions require independent corroboration and policy-based approval, regardless of apparent seniority.
questions.keyTakeaway: For high-impact financial changes, verify identity and authorization outside the channel carrying the request.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Pause payment, use contact details already held in trusted records, validate the beneficiary independently and retain the approval trail.
questions.difficultyRationale: Advanced level: organizational prioritization, governance or cross-functional judgment.

questions.title: The executive voice instruction
questions.learningObjective: Use independent identity verification when voice or video may be synthetically generated
questions.scenario: An audio message sounds like the CFO and requests an urgent transfer. The voice is convincing, but the request is unusual and asks you to bypass standard approvals.
questions.question: What is the most defensible response?

options.text: Ask a question about a public detail to test the caller.
Forward the audio to colleagues and let them vote on whether it sounds real.
Trust the voice because it resembles the CFO.
Verify through a separate known channel and enforce normal payment approvals; treat the recording as untrusted evidence.

questions.correctAnswer: Verify through a separate known channel and enforce normal payment approvals; treat the recording as untrusted evidence.

A.explanation: Public details may be available to an impersonator and provide weak authentication.

B.explanation: Human familiarity is not reliable deepfake detection and crowdsourcing delays the control response.

C.explanation: Voice similarity is not sufficient proof when synthetic impersonation is possible.

D.explanation: Correct. Independent identity checks and process controls remain effective even when media appears convincing.

questions.explanation: Correct. Independent identity checks and process controls remain effective even when media appears convincing.
questions.keyTakeaway: Authentic-sounding audio or video is not a trusted authentication factor for a high-impact request.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Use a known number or in-person confirmation, a pre-agreed verification phrase where appropriate, and standard dual controls; report the impersonation attempt.
questions.difficultyRationale: Advanced level: organizational prioritization, governance or cross-functional judgment.

questions.title: Unusual data exports
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish observable policy-relevant indicators from unsupported assumptions about intent
questions.scenario: A staff member with legitimate access downloads an unusually large volume of project files outside their normal work pattern. There is no evidence yet of data exfiltration or malicious intent.
questions.question: What is the appropriate organizational response?

options.text: Preserve relevant authorized telemetry and route the observable anomaly to the designated security/insider-risk process for proportionate review.
Search the employee’s personal devices without authorization.
Publicly accuse the employee of stealing data.
Ignore it because the employee is authorized to access the files.

questions.correctAnswer: Preserve relevant authorized telemetry and route the observable anomaly to the designated security/insider-risk process for proportionate review.

A.explanation: Correct. Focus on verifiable behavior, policy and authorized investigation, not unsupported personal assumptions.

B.explanation: Unapproved surveillance or access can violate law, policy and privacy; follow authorized procedures.

C.explanation: Anomalous activity is not proof of intent; public accusation can harm fairness and compromise an investigation.

D.explanation: Authorized access can still be misused or become anomalous; the activity may warrant review.

questions.explanation: Correct. Focus on verifiable behavior, policy and authorized investigation, not unsupported personal assumptions.
questions.keyTakeaway: An indicator is a reason for proportionate review—not a diagnosis of motive or guilt.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Preserve relevant logs according to policy, report through designated channels, limit information to need-to-know reviewers and involve HR/legal/privacy as required.
questions.difficultyRationale: Advanced level: organizational prioritization, governance or cross-functional judgment.

questions.title: The compromised privileged account
questions.learningObjective: Prioritize containment, credential revocation and trusted recovery after suspected compromise
questions.scenario: A privileged administrator reports a suspicious login. Audit records show a new session and unfamiliar mailbox forwarding rule. The user’s password may be compromised.
questions.question: Which response sequence is best?

options.text: Delete all logs and forwarding rules before contacting security.
Ask the administrator to change the password and continue normal work.
Disable every employee account across the organization.
Coordinate incident response: contain access, revoke affected sessions/tokens, secure credentials and recovery factors, preserve evidence, and investigate persistence.

questions.correctAnswer: Coordinate incident response: contain access, revoke affected sessions/tokens, secure credentials and recovery factors, preserve evidence, and investigate persistence.

A.explanation: Deleting evidence can obstruct investigation and may remove only visible indicators.

B.explanation: Password change alone may leave active sessions, tokens, forwarding rules or attacker persistence in place.

C.explanation: A broad disruptive response without scope assessment may cause unnecessary outage and is not proportionate.

D.explanation: Correct. Account compromise requires coordinated containment and recovery, not only a password change.

questions.explanation: Correct. Account compromise requires coordinated containment and recovery, not only a password change.
questions.keyTakeaway: After suspected credential compromise, address sessions, tokens, recovery paths and persistence as well as the password.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Activate the incident-response process, coordinate identity and system owners, contain the affected account, preserve evidence and verify recovery before restoring access.
questions.difficultyRationale: Advanced level: organizational prioritization, governance or cross-functional judgment.

questions.title: Two competing incidents
questions.learningObjective: Prioritize incidents by impact, exposure, time sensitivity and containment needs
questions.scenario: An organization has two alerts: (A) malware is actively encrypting files on a shared operational server; (B) a single employee received a suspicious email but did not open it. Both require triage.
questions.question: Which prioritization is most defensible?

options.text: Wait until both investigations are complete before taking action.
Prioritize the email because phishing is the most common initial-access vector.
Treat both as identical because each is a cybersecurity alert.
Prioritize the active encryption event for immediate coordinated containment while ensuring the email is reported and triaged.

questions.correctAnswer: Prioritize the active encryption event for immediate coordinated containment while ensuring the email is reported and triaged.

A.explanation: Delaying containment during active encryption may increase damage.

B.explanation: General prevalence does not outweigh evidence of active encryption and immediate operational impact.

C.explanation: Incidents differ in impact, scope, active harm and urgency; equal priority is not risk-based.

D.explanation: Correct. Active disruption and potential spread represent immediate operational risk; the lower-impact email still needs handling.

questions.explanation: Correct. Active disruption and potential spread represent immediate operational risk; the lower-impact email still needs handling.
questions.keyTakeaway: Prioritization considers current impact, scope, exposure, time sensitivity and containment opportunity.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Activate the incident-response plan, coordinate containment of the actively affected system, assign triage to the email and document priority rationale.
questions.difficultyRationale: Advanced level: organizational prioritization, governance or cross-functional judgment.

questions.title: The emergency MFA exception
questions.learningObjective: Apply policy exceptions through authorization, risk acceptance and documented controls
questions.scenario: A product team requests a six-month MFA exception for a production administrator account to simplify deployment. No compensating controls or accountable risk owner are proposed.
questions.question: What is the proper governance response?

options.text: Approve it because project delivery is time-critical.
Allow the team to use a shared administrator account instead.
Require documented business justification, scoped duration, risk-owner approval, compensating controls, monitoring and an expiry/review date before any exception.
Reject every exception without assessing context.

questions.correctAnswer: Require documented business justification, scoped duration, risk-owner approval, compensating controls, monitoring and an expiry/review date before any exception.

A.explanation: Schedule pressure alone does not justify accepting an undocumented security risk.

B.explanation: Shared privileged accounts weaken accountability and do not solve the underlying control gap.

C.explanation: Correct. A controlled exception process preserves accountability and makes residual risk explicit.

D.explanation: Some exceptions may be justified, but they require formal risk assessment, approval and compensating controls.

questions.explanation: Correct. A controlled exception process preserves accountability and makes residual risk explicit.
questions.keyTakeaway: An exception is a governed risk decision, not an informal bypass.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Use the organization’s exception workflow, define the account and period in scope, assess residual risk, assign an accountable approver and set a review/expiry date.
questions.difficultyRationale: Advanced level: organizational prioritization, governance or cross-functional judgment.

questions.title: The risk register decision
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate likelihood, impact, existing controls and residual risk systematically
questions.scenario: A risk register lists a low-likelihood event that could expose a large customer database. Existing controls are documented, but their current effectiveness has not been tested.
questions.question: What is the most sound assessment approach?

options.text: Mark the risk low because the event is unlikely.
Assess likelihood and impact, validate existing control effectiveness, estimate residual risk and record assumptions and uncertainty.
Mark the risk critical because all data incidents are critical.
Remove it from the register because controls are documented.

questions.correctAnswer: Assess likelihood and impact, validate existing control effectiveness, estimate residual risk and record assumptions and uncertainty.

A.explanation: Low likelihood alone ignores potentially severe impact and uncertainty about control effectiveness.

B.explanation: Correct. Risk assessment should consider both likelihood and consequence, then evaluate how controls change residual exposure.

C.explanation: Automatic maximum ratings do not provide a consistent or useful risk prioritization method.

D.explanation: Documented controls are not necessarily effective; the risk remains until assessed and treated appropriately.

questions.explanation: Correct. Risk assessment should consider both likelihood and consequence, then evaluate how controls change residual exposure.
questions.keyTakeaway: Risk decisions require likelihood, impact, control evidence, residual risk and explicit assumptions.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Validate control operation, document evidence and uncertainty, calculate or qualitatively rate residual risk, then assign treatment and ownership.
questions.difficultyRationale: Advanced level: organizational prioritization, governance or cross-functional judgment.

questions.title: The vendor integration request
questions.learningObjective: Assess supplier access, assurance evidence and data-handling obligations
questions.scenario: A supplier asks for broad administrator access to your cloud tenant to troubleshoot an integration. The contract does not clearly describe data processing, logging or access termination.
questions.question: What should the organization require before granting access?

options.text: Complete supplier/security review, define data and access scope, use named time-bound least-privilege accounts, log activity and document offboarding.
Grant the requested access for convenience and review it later.
Create a shared administrator password and send it over email.
Ask the vendor to promise that it will not access unrelated data.

questions.correctAnswer: Complete supplier/security review, define data and access scope, use named time-bound least-privilege accounts, log activity and document offboarding.

A.explanation: Correct. Supplier access should be constrained, attributable, monitored and governed by explicit contractual and technical controls.

B.explanation: Broad access before due diligence expands exposure and can be difficult to unwind.

C.explanation: Shared credentials reduce accountability and create an insecure secret-distribution path.

D.explanation: A verbal promise without enforceable scope and technical controls is insufficient.

questions.explanation: Correct. Supplier access should be constrained, attributable, monitored and governed by explicit contractual and technical controls.
questions.keyTakeaway: Third-party trust must be supported by evidence, scoped access, monitoring and lifecycle controls.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Delay access until procurement, security, privacy and system owners document the supplier’s need, safeguards, data terms, account scope and revocation plan.
questions.difficultyRationale: Advanced level: organizational prioritization, governance or cross-functional judgment.

questions.title: The misdirected personal-data file
questions.learningObjective: Limit exposure, preserve relevant facts and notify responsible privacy/security roles
questions.scenario: A staff member emails a spreadsheet with personal identifiers to an external recipient with a similar name. The recipient has not yet confirmed deletion.
questions.question: What is the best immediate response?

options.text: Send a follow-up asking the recipient to delete it and close the matter.
Notify the privacy/security incident channel promptly, preserve message details, request containment through approved procedures and let authorized roles assess notification obligations.
Recall the email and delete the sent copy, then assume the risk is resolved.
Send the file to a larger group so the error is transparent.

questions.correctAnswer: Notify the privacy/security incident channel promptly, preserve message details, request containment through approved procedures and let authorized roles assess notification obligations.

A.explanation: A deletion request may help but does not replace formal incident assessment, notification and evidence preservation.

B.explanation: Correct. Prompt escalation allows the organization to assess exposure, legal/contractual duties and necessary containment.

C.explanation: Recall may fail or the recipient may already have accessed or copied the file.

D.explanation: Further disclosure increases exposure and is not an incident-response control.

questions.explanation: Correct. Prompt escalation allows the organization to assess exposure, legal/contractual duties and necessary containment.
questions.keyTakeaway: A misdirected data disclosure is an incident to assess even when accidental and even if recall is attempted.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Report immediately, preserve relevant facts without unnecessary copying, request approved recipient-side containment and follow the privacy team’s incident process.
questions.difficultyRationale: Advanced level: organizational prioritization, governance or cross-functional judgment.

questions.title: The investigation log request
questions.learningObjective: Use authorized logs and preserve relevant evidence without over-collecting personal data
questions.scenario: During an investigation, a manager asks you to export all employee browsing history and personal messages, although the incident concerns access to one cloud folder.
questions.question: What is the most defensible approach?

options.text: Refuse to provide any logs under all circumstances.
Modify timestamps to make the sequence easier to understand.
Work with authorized investigators to identify relevant log sources, scope, retention and access controls; preserve integrity and document handling.
Export everything because more data always helps an investigation.

questions.correctAnswer: Work with authorized investigators to identify relevant log sources, scope, retention and access controls; preserve integrity and document handling.

A.explanation: Authorized, proportionate logs may be necessary for a legitimate investigation.

B.explanation: Altering original evidence destroys integrity and undermines investigative reliability.

C.explanation: Correct. Evidence collection should be authorized, relevant, minimized and handled with integrity.

D.explanation: Over-collection creates privacy, security and proportionality risks and may exceed the investigation’s authorization.

questions.explanation: Correct. Evidence collection should be authorized, relevant, minimized and handled with integrity.
questions.keyTakeaway: Collect the minimum authorized evidence needed, preserve integrity and record chain of handling.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Confirm authority and scope, preserve source records, restrict access, record collection metadata and involve privacy/legal roles where required.
questions.difficultyRationale: Advanced level: organizational prioritization, governance or cross-functional judgment.

questions.title: The AI-generated incident advisory
questions.learningObjective: Review AI-generated security guidance for fabricated claims, bias and unsafe recommendations
questions.scenario: An AI assistant produces an incident-response memo citing a non-existent CVE and recommending a command that would disable endpoint protection across all workstations.
questions.question: What should the security lead do?

options.text: Distribute it because the memo includes citations and technical language.
Treat it as an unverified draft, validate every source and recommendation against authoritative advisories and approved procedures, and reject unsafe actions.
Run the recommended command on a small sample of production devices.
Ask the same AI model to confirm that its first answer was correct.

questions.correctAnswer: Treat it as an unverified draft, validate every source and recommendation against authoritative advisories and approved procedures, and reject unsafe actions.

A.explanation: Citations and fluent technical prose do not establish factual accuracy or safety.

B.explanation: Correct. AI output needs provenance, technical validation, and human approval before it informs operational response.

C.explanation: Testing an unsafe command on production may still cause harm; validate in a controlled environment after expert review.

D.explanation: Self-confirmation by the same model is not independent evidence and may reproduce the original error.

questions.explanation: Correct. AI output needs provenance, technical validation, and human approval before it informs operational response.
questions.keyTakeaway: Generative AI can produce plausible but false or unsafe security guidance; verify independently before action.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Check identifiers in authoritative vulnerability databases and vendor advisories, test any safe proposed steps in a controlled environment, and require qualified human sign-off.
questions.difficultyRationale: Advanced level: organizational prioritization, governance or cross-functional judgment.

questions.title: The active ransomware event
questions.learningObjective: Prioritize isolation and incident escalation without destroying evidence or improvising recovery
questions.scenario: A workstation displays a ransom note, and several shared files are becoming inaccessible. The user asks whether to reboot the machine and delete the note.
questions.question: What should the incident coordinator prioritize?

options.text: Isolate affected systems in a coordinated manner, activate the response plan and preserve evidence; follow recovery guidance from authorized responders.
Connect an external backup drive to copy files from the affected workstation.
Reboot all affected systems immediately.
Delete the ransom note and pay from a personal account.

questions.correctAnswer: Isolate affected systems in a coordinated manner, activate the response plan and preserve evidence; follow recovery guidance from authorized responders.

A.explanation: Correct. Containment is urgent, but should be coordinated; evidence and recovery decisions must be handled through incident response.

B.explanation: Connecting removable media to a potentially infected machine may expose backups to compromise.

C.explanation: Uncoordinated rebooting may destroy volatile evidence and does not reliably stop propagation.

D.explanation: Deleting evidence is harmful, and payment is not a reliable recovery strategy or unilateral user decision.

questions.explanation: Correct. Containment is urgent, but should be coordinated; evidence and recovery decisions must be handled through incident response.
questions.keyTakeaway: Contain ransomware safely and coordinate response; do not improvise recovery or destroy evidence.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Activate the incident-response process, isolate affected systems as directed, protect clean backups, preserve evidence and involve system owners and authorities as appropriate.
questions.difficultyRationale: Advanced level: organizational prioritization, governance or cross-functional judgment.

questions.title: The over-privileged analyst
questions.learningObjective: Apply least privilege, segregation of duties and timely access review
questions.scenario: A data analyst has permanent administrator access to payroll, identity management and production infrastructure, although their role only requires read-only access to one reporting dataset.
questions.question: Which access-governance action is most appropriate?

options.text: Replace the account with a shared team administrator account.
Remove unnecessary privileges, grant a named read-only role for the required dataset and review access periodically.
Keep the access because the analyst is trusted.
Allow the analyst to retain admin access but ask them not to use it.

questions.correctAnswer: Remove unnecessary privileges, grant a named read-only role for the required dataset and review access periodically.

A.explanation: Shared privileged accounts reduce accountability and do not implement least privilege.

B.explanation: Correct. Access should be limited to the minimum necessary resources and authorizations for assigned tasks.

C.explanation: Trust does not replace role-based need, segregation of duties or periodic authorization review.

D.explanation: Unused privilege remains available for accidental misuse or account compromise.

questions.explanation: Correct. Access should be limited to the minimum necessary resources and authorizations for assigned tasks.
questions.keyTakeaway: Grant each identity only the access needed for its assigned function, and review it as roles change.
questions.recommendedDefensiveAction: Use named accounts and scoped roles, remove excess privileges, segregate incompatible duties and schedule access recertification.
questions.difficultyRationale: Advanced level: organizational prioritization, governance or cross-functional judgment.

questions.title: Choosing authentication for high-risk administrators
questions.learningObjective: Select phishing-resistant authentication for high-risk contexts and address fallback risks
questions.scenario: An organization is redesigning authentication for privileged administrators. Options include password plus SMS OTP, push approval, or phishing-resistant public-key authentication, but legacy recovery remains weak.
questions.question: Which design is strongest?

options.text: Use push approval with unlimited prompts and no number/context matching.
Use password plus SMS OTP for every administrator and leave recovery unchanged.
Adopt phishing-resistant authentication such as FIDO/WebAuthn for privileged access and harden enrollment, recovery and fallback paths.
Remove MFA and rely only on a longer password.

questions.title: Vishing: safest response
questions.learningObjective: Respond safely to voice-based impersonation and requests for authentication secrets.
questions.scenario: A caller claiming to be the university helpdesk says a sign-in attack is underway and asks the student to read a one-time verification code aloud.
questions.question: Which response is the safest and most appropriate next step?

options.text: Accept the request as routine and complete it without a separate check.
End the call and contact the helpdesk using the number on the official university website; never disclose the code.
Wait until a confirmed loss, outage or policy violation appears before acting.
Share the full details with a broad group so others can decide informally.

questions.correctAnswer: End the call and contact the helpdesk using the number on the official university website; never disclose the code.

A.explanation: A routine-looking request does not establish the source’s identity or the action’s authorization; independent verification is still required.

B.explanation: This directly addresses callers can impersonate support or authority figures to solicit codes or actions. The proposed action uses approved, independently verifiable controls: End the call and contact the helpdesk using the number on the official university website; never disclose the code.

C.explanation: Waiting for visible harm can extend the exposure and delay proportionate prevention, containment or reporting.

D.explanation: Broad circulation can expose sensitive information or spread unsafe content; use an approved need-to-know process.

questions.question: Which evidence provides the strongest basis for that decision?

options.text: The caller knows the student’s name and department.
The incoming number displays the university name.
A callback to the helpdesk number independently obtained from the official directory and a matching support-ticket record.
The caller says the code will expire in one minute.

questions.correctAnswer: A callback to the helpdesk number independently obtained from the official directory and a matching support-ticket record.
